body.h2: Summary
body.text: 6 November 2020

body.h2: Summary
body.text: The British population has been asked about the impacts that the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has had on their lives, and how they are coping. The latest findings are published in our weekly bulletin [Coronavirus and the social impacts on Great Britain](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/bulletins/coronavirusandthesocialimpactsongreatbritain/latest).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: With various restrictions in place across Great Britain in the latest week (28 October to 1 November 2020), around 7 in 10 (71%) adults said that they strongly support or tend to support the use of targeted lockdown measures for local areas affected by coronavirus outbreaks; this percentage has been declining since the end of September (82% over the period 30 September to 4 October).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: We also found this week that a lower percentage of those who were in higher tier levels in England reported that they had enough information about government plans to manage the coronavirus pandemic (Tier 2: 37% and Tier 3: 34%). This compares with 45% of those in Tier 1.

body.h2: Summary
body.text: Rising COVID-19 infections and the reintroduction of some restrictions appear to have had an impact on general well-being. Life satisfaction scores were at their lowest (6.5 out of 10) since the survey started, and happiness scores continued to decrease for the third week in a row (6.7 out of 10).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: Similar proportions of people across each of the local COVID alert areas reported that they are very or somewhat worried about the effect of the coronavirus on their life right now (76% in Tier 1, 77% in Tier 2, 78% in Tier 3). However, there were some differences in concerns reported between the alert areas. The concerns with the largest differences between those in Tier 3 and those in Tier 1 were the lack of freedom and independence (68% and 57% respectively) and well-being (for example, boredom, loneliness, anxiety, and stress) (57% and 50% respectively).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: View our summaries of [death and health](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundupdeathsandhealth/2020-06-26) and [economic impacts](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundupeconomybusinessandjobs/2020-07-02), or go to our [main roundup page for the latest across all topics](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundup/2020-03-26).

body.h2: Summary
body.text: This page is a summary of insights from our most recent analysis and will be updated as new publications are released. [Sign up to our email alerts for daily updates](https://public.govdelivery.com/accounts/UKONS/subscribers/new) in your inbox.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: More than three-quarters (77%) of adults in the North West of England reported they have been living under the most stringent local coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown measure.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: The government’s local COVID-19 alert system was introduced on 12 October, 2020 and classified local areas under a ”tier” system.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: Different rules applied in different parts of the country for meeting up with others outside their household or support bubble, of which the majority of the North West was in Tier 3.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: A second national lockdown for England, started on 5 November, before responses for this survey for the period 28 October to 1 November 2020, were collected.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: Under the alert system, according to the [latest Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN)](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/bulletins/coronavirusandthesocialimpactsongreatbritain/latest), the region with the highest proportion of adults reporting living under Tier 2 restrictions was the North East, with 95%.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: The South West had the highest proportion (93%) of people reporting they were living in the lowest level of restrictions, Tier 1.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.chartbuilder_h3: Nearly 8 in 10 adults in the North West self-reported that they were in Tier 3

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: This week, we asked adults about the rules that applied where they live. In Tier 1, 89% of adults identified with the rule that people must not meet in groups larger than six indoors.

body.h2: Regional differences in local COVID-19 alert system
body.text: In Tier 2 and Tier 3, the majority of adults (73% and 80% respectively) identified with the rule that people must not meet indoors with others from outside their household.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: Crime decreased at height of lockdown

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: There has been a 19% decrease in the number of victims of [crime in England and Wales between April and June 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/crimeinenglandandwalesyearendingjune2020), compared with the same period in 2019.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: Statistics from the Telephone-operated Crime Survey for England and Wales (TCSEW) show that the decrease in overall crime, during the height of the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown, was largely driven by a 30% drop in thefts overall, compared with the previous quarter in 2020.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: The lockdown, which was implemented at the end of March 2020, prompted a societal change, in that people were staying at home, making it difficult for theft crimes to be committed.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.chartbuilder_h3: Falling TCSEW victimisation levels during April to June 2020 were driven by large decreases in theft offences
body.chartbuilder_h4: England and Wales, based on interviews conducted between May and August 2020

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: Total police recorded crime decreased by 4% in England and Wales to approximately 5.8 million offences in the 12 months ending June 2020; the annual decrease was mainly driven by substantial falls during the April to June 2020 period, particularly in theft offences.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: The quarter from April to June 2020 also saw a 43% drop in theft offences and a 47% drop in robberies, compared with April to June 2019. This reflects the increase in time people spent at home during the lockdown, reducing opportunities for theft in public spaces, and the closure of the night-time economy.

body.h2: Crime decreased at height of lockdown
body.text: By contrast, recorded drug offences rose by 30% in April to June 2020 (57,132 offences) compared with April to June 2019. This reflected proactive police activity in crime hotspots and was largely driven by offences involving the possession of drugs.

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: Six months ago, lockdown measures were introduced in Great Britain to slow the spread of the coronavirus (COVID-19) and throughout this time, we have been asking people about their opinions and behaviours.

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: [We have now presented people’s experiences in their own words](https://www.ons.gov.uk/visualisations/dvc983/Diary_of_a_nation-20200907082746841/index.html), capturing how people across the country have been coping with the many changes brought about by the pandemic.
body.text_new: [We have now presented people’s experiences in their own words](https://onsdigital.github.io/visualisations/dvc983/Diary_of_a_nation-20200907082746841/index.html), capturing how people across the country have been coping with the many changes brought about by the pandemic.

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: In March, more than half of adults said they thought life would be back to normal within six months. However, when the same question was posed to people in August, “more than a year” was the most popular response, with over a third (37%) of adults saying they thought this is how long the pandemic would last.

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: The uncertainty people faced was clear to see in the survey’s free text responses, which we now present for the first time. One person said their life was “on hold” during self-isolation, while another said they lacked “any idea about when and how things might ‘return to normal’”.

body.h2: Diary of a nation: life in lockdown
body.text: Following five months of restrictions, and the end of the pandemic still not in sight, a third of adults said they felt COVID-19 was the most important issue facing Britain. However, others have expressed positive outcomes from the last six months, such as one respondent who said they “appreciate the little things that matter more” and another who said they were enjoying a “more thoughtful and engaging lifestyle”.

body.h2: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety
body.text: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety

body.h2: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety
body.text: Our [latest bulletin on personal and economic well-being in Great Britain](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/bulletins/personalandeconomicwellbeingintheuk/latest) during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic explores how different people fared as lockdown restrictions eased, using results from the Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN). OPN has been collecting data on the impact of COVID-19 on day-to-day life in Great Britain since 20 March 2020.

body.h2: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety
body.text: During June and early July 2020, more people returned to work, particularly those in the £10,000 to £20,000 income bracket. However, since mid-July, when three out of four employed people were back in work, this trend levelled off – though may be due to some people taking time off in the summer.

body.h2: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety
body.text: Despite the gradual easing of lockdown restrictions, the number of people who thought that it would take more than a year for things to return to normal, if at all, started to increase again during July.

body.h2: Returning to work, household finances and anxiety
body.text: The bulletin also looks at how people fared financially. Around one in four people in employment reported reduced household income at the end of May, which declined to one in six and then stayed flat from mid-July.

body.text: While improvements in finances stalled, financial resilience worsened throughout July, with one-third of the population reporting they were not able to find money for an unexpected but necessary expense by the end of the month. Parents and renters fared worse in this regard with around half of them unable to cover such an expense by the end of July, possibly because both groups were more likely to report reduced hours and not being able to work from home.

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: Return to school

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: More than half of parents of school-age children in England and Wales are worried about their children’s return to school next term.

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: [Adults with dependent children were asked a series of questions](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/bulletins/coronavirusandthesocialimpactsongreatbritain/latest) about the oldest school age child in their household returning to school or college and 52% said they were very worried or somewhat worried about it.

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: This did not dissuade most parents with school age children from wanting their children to go back to school. Almost all (97%) in England and Wales, said it was very likely or fairly likely that the oldest school age child in their household would return to school or college when school reopens to them in the new term.

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: The main concern (58%) reported by adults with children of school age in the next term, is that they are worried about the oldest age child in their household catching the coronavirus (COVID-19) at school or college.

body.h2: Return to school
body.text: Nearly half (46%) of parents said the oldest child in their household has mixed feelings about returning to school or college, however, an additional 36% said they were looking forward to returning to school or college.

body.h2: International travel
body.text: Restrictions on international travel have been in place since early 2020 because of the coronavirus (COVID-19). Recently, [the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) have started to ease travel restrictions for British travellers](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/coronavirus-covid-19-countries-and-territories-exempt-from-advice-against-all-but-essential-international-travel) where countries are assessed as “no longer presenting an unacceptably high risk to British people traveling abroad”. We have included analysis up to June 2020 of [recent international travel in our migration release.](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/migrationstatisticsquarterlyreport/august2020#insights-into-recent-international-travel-patterns)

body.h2: International travel
body.text: These insights are not measures of international migration as they refer to travel patterns by all types of passengers, not just international migrants.

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: As time has progressed through the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, [public perception on unity has altered](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/bulletins/unityanddivisioningreatbritain/24aprilto28june2020). Between 24 April and 28 June 2020 the weekly Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN) found that the percentage of adults who thought that Britain would be more united after the pandemic declined by 29 percentage points (from 57% in the first week of the period to 28% in the last week).

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: Over the period as a whole more people thought that Great Britain would be more united after the pandemic (46%) than before the outbreak (24%). When divided by nation, adults in Scotland were less likely (31%) to think Britain will be more united after the pandemic than those in England (47%) or Wales (44%).

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.h4: Although people in Scotland were more likely to think that Britain will be united after the coronavirus pandemic than to think it was united before, they were less likely to say this than those in England or Wales

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Our [survey in July](http://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/disability/articles/coronavirusandthesocialimpactsondisabledpeopleingreatbritain/july2020) showed that disabled people were more likely to be worried about the effect that the coronavirus (COVID-19) was having on their lives than non-disabled people. Three-quarters (75%) of disabled people said they were either “very worried” or “somewhat worried” compared with 66% of non-disabled people.

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Of the worries they had, almost one-quarter of disabled people were most concerned about the impact of the coronavirus on their well-being (24%) (13% for non-disabled people). Next most frequently, 13% of disabled people reported being most concerned about access to healthcare and treatment (compared with 3% of non-disabled people).

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Disabled people continue to experience poorer well-being ratings than before the pandemic started. In July 2020, 45% of disabled people reported high anxiety.

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: The survey results show that 25% of disabled people who were receiving medical care prior to the pandemic are receiving treatment for only some of their conditions, compared with 7% of non-disabled people in a similar situation.

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Similar proportions of disabled people (43%) and non-disabled people (44%) said they had received visitors at their home. However, more disabled people told us they had not met up with other people than non-disabled people – 37% compared with 29% respectively.

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: Although more disabled people had left their home for some reason in July than May 2020, the proportion was still lower than non-disabled people. In July, 95% of non-disabled people had left their home for some reason compared with 87% of disabled people.

body.h2: Disabled people were most concerned about the impacts of coronavirus on their well-being and access to healthcare in July 2020
body.text: One reason for this difference might be because fewer disabled people (17%) report feeling safe outside their home than non-disabled people (27%).

body.text: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: The guidance for clinically extremely vulnerable (CEV) people has changed in recent weeks. This is reflected in the responses to our Shielding Behavioural Survey.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: [Our latest survey was carried out between 9 and 16 July.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/bulletins/coronavirusandshieldingofclinicallyextremelyvulnerablepeopleinengland/latest) It shows more CEV people are leaving their home and receiving visitors at their home.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: Almost half (48%) of CEV people report not leaving their home at all or only leaving for exercise. This is lower than the 60% of people who said the same in [the previous survey between 24 and 30 June.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/bulletins/coronavirusandshieldingofclinicallyextremelyvulnerablepeopleinengland/24juneto30june2020)

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: The percentage of CEV people receiving no visitors at their home (other than for support for personal care) has decreased in each of the past three surveys. [Between 28 May and 3 June,](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/bulletins/coronavirusandshieldingofclinicallyextremelyvulnerablepeopleinengland/28mayto3june2020) 87% of CEV people told us they had not received visitors at their home. This fell to 83% in [the next survey (9 to 18 June)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/bulletins/coronavirusandshieldingofclinicallyextremelyvulnerablepeopleinengland/9juneto18june2020), then 77% in the following one (24 to 30 June).

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: On 6 July, guidance for CEV people shielding changed to include forming a support bubble with another household. In our latest survey, 65% of CEV people reported receiving no visitors to their home (other than support for personal care).

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.text: Fifteen percent of CEV people live with someone under the age of 16 years. A fifth of those said living with children is impacting their ability to shield.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance

body.text: CEV shielding workers

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: Over a quarter (28%) of CEV people who were advised to shield were in employment before lockdown. Of that 28% of CEV people:

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: 11% continued to work outside their home

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: 37% now work from home

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: the remaining 52% were either furloughed, joined the self-employed income support scheme or stopped working

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: An estimated 38,000 (6%) CEV people who worked before lockdown said they would not return to work in the next four months. A fifth (21%) of CEV workers said they would continue to work from home for the next four months. That’s down from the 37% who said they are working at home now.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: Almost one in four (23%) CEV workers said they didn’t know what their plans were for the coming four months.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: There is some variation in how comfortable CEV people are with returning to work outside their homes.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: More than two thirds (68%) of CEV workers said they were comfortable (44%) or completely comfortable (24%) with returning to work outside their home. However, their comfort level was dependent on protective measures being in place.

body.h2: Shielding behaviours changing with updated guidance
body.h4: CEV shielding workers
body.text: In comparison, 32% of CEV workers said they are not comfortable with returning to work outside their home.
